LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometry & Flow:
Spirometry is the core bedside pulmonary function test, measuring the volume and speed of air a patient can forcibly exhale to classify lung disease into obstructive and restrictive patterns. By comparing the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV₁), the forced vital capacity (FVC) and their ratio, it distinguishes airflow limitation (COPD, asthma) from reduced lung expansion (fibrosis, chest-wall and neuromuscular disease), guiding diagnosis, severity grading and treatment.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Spirometry is indicated for investigating chronic breathlessness, cough or wheeze, and for diagnosing and monitoring COPD, asthma and interstitial lung disease. It rests on three measurements from a single maximal forced blow.

🧪FEV₁
Volume exhaled in the first second — falls with airflow limitation
🫁FVC
Total volume forcibly exhaled from full inspiration — falls in restriction
📊FEV₁/FVC
The ratio — the key discriminator between obstruction and restriction
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Patient seated, nose-clip applied, mouth sealed around the mouthpiece; short-acting bronchodilators withheld beforehand where reversibility is being assessed.
A maximal inspiration to total lung capacity is followed by a fast, forced and complete exhalation lasting ≥6 seconds until a plateau is reached.
ATS/ERS acceptability requires a good start (no hesitation), no cough in the first second and no early termination.
At least 3 acceptable blows are needed; repeatability requires the best two FEV₁ and best two FVC values within 150 mL of each other.
3INTERPRETATION — THE PATTERNS

The FEV₁/FVC ratio is read first: a low ratio defines obstruction, a preserved or raised ratio points to restriction.

FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 (or below LLN), FEV₁ reduced→OBSTRUCTIVE pattern — COPD, asthma
FVC reduced, FEV₁/FVC normal or raised (≥ 0.70)→RESTRICTIVE pattern — confirm with reduced TLC on lung volumes
FEV₁ increase ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL post-bronchodilator→Significant reversibility — favours asthma over COPD
Both FEV₁ and FVC low with low ratio→Possible mixed pattern — needs full lung volumes

Causes cluster by pattern:

💨COPD
Obstructive, typically irreversible airflow limitation
🌬️Asthma
Obstructive with significant bronchodilator reversibility
🕸️Fibrosis
Restrictive — interstitial lung disease reduces expansion
🦴Chest wall
Restrictive — kyphoscoliosis, obesity limit chest movement
⚡Neuromuscular
Restrictive — weak respiratory muscles (e.g. motor neurone disease)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Effort-dependent: submaximal effort or poor technique produces spuriously low values and a false restrictive appearance.
The fixed 0.70 ratio over-diagnoses obstruction in the elderly and under-diagnoses it in the young; the lower limit of normal (LLN) accounts for age, sex, height and ethnicity.
A low FVC alone does NOT confirm restriction — it may reflect gas trapping in severe obstruction; true restriction needs a reduced TLC on body plethysmography or gas dilution.
🚩 Restriction cannot be diagnosed on spirometry alone. A reduced FVC with a preserved ratio only suggests it — confirmation requires lung volumes showing a reduced total lung capacity (TLC). Beware the mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern where both FEV₁ and FVC fall and spirometry alone is misleading.
🎓 Read the ratio first. FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 = obstruction; a normal or raised ratio with a low FVC = (suspected) restriction. Significant bronchodilator reversibility (FEV₁ up ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL) points to asthma rather than COPD.

Spirometry cannot be read against a single number — a "normal" FEV1 for a 22-year-old 190 cm man is grossly abnormal for a 75-year-old 150 cm woman. Reference (predicted) values convert a raw measurement into a statement about whether that individual's lungs are normal for a person of the same age, height, sex and ethnicity. The Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI) 2012 equations are the internationally endorsed reference set, and the lower limit of normal (LLN) — not a fixed cut-off — defines the boundary of health.

1WHY PREDICTED VALUES DEPEND ON AGE, HEIGHT, SEX & ETHNICITY
Height is the strongest determinant — lung volumes scale with body size, so taller people have larger FEV1 and FVC.
Age — volumes rise through childhood, plateau in the early 20s, then decline steadily (elastic recoil falls, chest wall stiffens).
Sex — males have larger lungs and airways for a given height.
Ethnicity — body build (sitting-height to leg-length ratio) differs between populations; ignoring it mislabels normal lungs as restricted. GLI supplies coefficients for Caucasian, African-American, North-East Asian and South-East Asian groups plus an "other/mixed" composite.
2THE GLI 2012 EQUATIONS & HOW A RESULT IS EXPRESSED
GLI-2012 pooled >74,000 healthy non-smokers aged 3–95 into one continuous model, removing the artificial discontinuity older equations had at age 18. For each index (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) the software returns three numbers:
📊Predicted (mean)
The average value for a healthy person of that age, height, sex & ethnicity.
📈% predicted
Measured ÷ predicted × 100. Intuitive but its "normal" range shifts with age & height.
🎯z-score
Number of standard deviations from the predicted mean — age/height/sex independent.
The z-score is preferred because it accounts for the fact that the scatter of normal values itself changes with age, which a flat "80% of predicted" rule cannot.
3THE LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL (LLN) = 5th CENTILE
By convention the LLN is set at the 5th centile of the healthy reference distribution — i.e. only 5% of genuinely healthy people fall below it (the accepted false-positive rate). On the z-score scale this is a fixed, memorable value:
z-score ≥ -1.64→Within normal limits
z-score < -1.64 (below the 5th centile)→Below the LLN — abnormal for this individual
FEV1/FVC z-score < -1.64→Airflow obstruction
FVC z-score < -1.64 with normal ratio→Suggests a restrictive pattern (confirm with lung volumes)
Because the LLN tracks the reference distribution at every age, it keeps the false-positive rate constant across the lifespan — the key advantage over any fixed threshold.
4FIXED RATIO 0.70 vs LLN — AND SEVERITY GRADING
GOLD uses a fixed post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 to define obstruction. Because the ratio physiologically falls with age, this fixed line diverges from the true 5th centile:
Elderly patient, ratio 0.68→Fixed ratio calls it "obstructed" — but may be > LLN (normal ageing): OVER-diagnosis
Young adult, ratio 0.72→Fixed ratio calls it "normal" — but may be < LLN: UNDER-diagnosis / missed early disease
Once obstruction is confirmed, severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted:
FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted→Mild (GOLD 1)
FEV1 50–79% predicted→Moderate (GOLD 2)
FEV1 30–49% predicted→Severe (GOLD 3)
FEV1 < 30% predicted→Very severe (GOLD 4)
🚩 Do not diagnose COPD on a fixed FEV1/FVC < 0.70 alone. In the elderly this over-diagnoses obstruction and labels healthy ageing lungs as diseased, exposing patients to unnecessary inhalers; in young adults it under-diagnoses and misses early disease. Always interpret against the GLI LLN (z < -1.64), and confirm airflow obstruction post-bronchodilator.
🎓 Remember the anchor: LLN = 5th centile = z-score of -1.64 for every index at every age. A z-score "normalises" the result so that -1.64 always means the same thing whether the patient is 8 or 80 — which is exactly why a single fixed % predicted or a fixed 0.70 ratio cannot.

Bronchodilator reversibility testing is a spirometry-based dynamic test that measures the change in airflow after inhaling a short-acting bronchodilator. It is used to demonstrate a reversible (variable) airflow component — the hallmark of asthma — and to help distinguish asthma from the largely fixed obstruction of COPD.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Performed when obstructive spirometry (FEV₁/FVC < 0.70) is found and the clinician needs to know how much of that obstruction can be relieved. In asthma, airway smooth-muscle contraction is a major, reversible driver of obstruction, so a β₂-agonist produces a marked rise in flow. In COPD the obstruction is dominated by fixed structural change (loss of elastic recoil, luminal remodelling), so any response is typically small.
Confirms a reversible component and supports a diagnosis of asthma.
Helps separate asthma from COPD and informs the choice of inhaled therapy.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Record baseline post-bronchodilator-free spirometry (best of three technically acceptable blows). Administer a short-acting bronchodilator — commonly 400 mcg inhaled salbutamol, ideally via a spacer. Repeat spirometry after an adequate interval.
Salbutamol 400 mcg→Repeat FEV₁ / FVC at 15–20 min
Short-acting antimuscarinic (ipratropium)→Repeat at 30–45 min instead
Bronchodilators must be withheld beforehand so baseline is not already dilated: short-acting agents for ~6 h, long-acting β₂-agonists for ~12–24 h, and long-acting antimuscarinics for ~36–48 h per local protocol.
3INTERPRETATION & THRESHOLDS
The improvement is compared against defined significance thresholds.
ATS/ERS 2022: change > 10% of predicted (FEV₁ or FVC)→Significant reversibility
Older criterion: ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL rise in FEV₁→Significant reversibility (still widely quoted)
Large response (e.g. FEV₁ rise ≥ 400 mL)→Strongly favours asthma
Little or no change with persistent obstruction→Favours COPD (fixed obstruction)
🫁Asthma
Marked reversibility; obstruction can normalise
🚬COPD
Minimal change; obstruction persists post-dose
🧪FEV₁
Primary index of airflow change
💨FVC
Rise can unmask air-trapping reversal
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Reversibility is variable day to day, so a single negative test never rules out asthma; response may also overlap between conditions. Poor inhaler technique, an inadequate dose, or failing to withhold prior bronchodilators can blunt or mask a true response. Interpret alongside history, peak-flow variability, and other objective tests rather than in isolation.
🚩 A negative bronchodilator reversibility test does NOT exclude asthma. Asthmatic airflow limitation is variable and may be near-normal at the time of testing — pursue further objective evidence (peak-flow diary, FeNO, or bronchial challenge) before discarding the diagnosis.
🎓 Remember two numbers: the classic threshold is ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL improvement in FEV₁, while the newer ATS/ERS 2022 criterion is a change > 10% of the predicted value for FEV₁ or FVC. A very large response (≥ 400 mL) points strongly toward asthma.

A flow–volume loop is a spirometry plot of airflow (y-axis, L/s) against lung volume (x-axis, L) through a single forced expiration followed by a forced inspiration. Its shape is diagnostic: the contour of each limb reveals not only whether disease is obstructive or restrictive, but—uniquely—can localise large (upper) airway obstruction to an intrathoracic, extrathoracic, or fixed lesion, often before any structural imaging.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Ordered to characterise dyspnoea, stridor, or an abnormal spirometry ratio, and to distinguish diffuse airways disease from a discrete central-airway lesion. The physiological basis is that transmural pressure across the airway wall differs between inspiration and expiration and differs above versus below the thoracic inlet.

Expiration: pleural pressure turns positive → compresses intrathoracic airways, but positive intraluminal pressure holds extrathoracic airways open.
Inspiration: pleural pressure turns negative → splints intrathoracic airways open, but negative intraluminal pressure tends to collapse extrathoracic airways.

A lesion that can change calibre with pressure is variable; a rigid lesion is fixed. This is why the plateau appears on the expiratory limb, the inspiratory limb, or both.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed on a calibrated spirometer with a nose clip and a tight mouthpiece seal. After a period of tidal breathing the patient inhales fully to total lung capacity, then performs a maximal forced expiration to residual volume, immediately followed by a maximal forced inspiration back to TLC—generating the closed loop.

By convention expiratory flow is plotted upward (above the volume axis) and inspiratory flow downward.
At least three technically acceptable, reproducible manoeuvres are recorded; peak flows should agree within tight tolerance to confirm maximal effort.
Poor effort or a leaking seal blunts peaks and can mimic a plateau, so technical quality must be confirmed before interpreting shape.
3INTERPRETATION — READING THE SHAPE

The normal loop has a rapid rise to a sharp expiratory peak (PEF) followed by a near-straight, gently sloping descent to RV, and a smooth semicircular inspiratory limb. Deviations from this contour define the pattern:

Concave / scooped-out expiratory limb, low PEF→Intrathoracic airflow OBSTRUCTION (e.g. asthma, COPD)
Tall, narrow, witch’s-hat loop shifted toward low volume→RESTRICTION — reduced volumes, preserved flow contour
Plateau on EXPIRATORY limb only→Variable INTRAthoracic large-airway obstruction
Plateau on INSPIRATORY limb only→Variable EXTRAthoracic obstruction (e.g. vocal cord dysfunction)
Plateau on BOTH limbs — box-like loop→FIXED large-airway obstruction (e.g. tracheal stenosis)
🫁Variable intrathoracic
Expiratory plateau; e.g. intrathoracic tracheal tumour, bronchomalacia
🗣️Variable extrathoracic
Inspiratory plateau; e.g. vocal cord dysfunction, extrathoracic tracheomalacia
📦Fixed obstruction
Both limbs plateaued; e.g. tracheal stenosis, large goitre, glottic tumour
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
The loop is effort- and technique-dependent; the inspiratory limb especially is often submaximal and can falsely suggest an extrathoracic plateau.
A useful quantitative clue to fixed/upper-airway obstruction is a FEF₅₀ : FIF₅₀ ratio ≥ 1 (expiratory flow at 50% volume relative to inspiratory flow at 50%).
Flow–volume loops localise and characterise but do not tissue-diagnose; a suspected central-airway lesion still needs direct visualisation and cross-sectional assessment.
🚩 Flattening (plateau) of either limb is a red flag for large-airway obstruction and is easily overlooked. A patient labelled “refractory asthma” with a flat inspiratory limb may have critical tracheal stenosis, a laryngeal tumour, or vocal cord dysfunction—forcing spirometry or sedating such a patient can precipitate complete airway occlusion.
🎓 Remember the pressure logic with one line: “Extrathoracic collapses on breathing IN, intrathoracic collapses on breathing OUT; if it collapses on both, it’s FIXED.” A box-shaped loop with plateaued inspiratory and expiratory limbs is the classic exam signature of fixed obstruction such as tracheal stenosis or a large retrosternal goitre.

Peak expiratory flow (PEF) is the maximum flow rate generated during a forced expiration from a position of full inflation, measured in litres per minute (L/min). It reflects flow through the large, effort-dependent airways and is a cheap, portable, reproducible bedside and home marker of large-airway calibre. Because it is measured repeatedly by patients themselves, serial PEF is used to diagnose asthma (by demonstrating variable airflow obstruction), to detect occupational asthma, and to grade the severity of an acute asthma attack against the patient's own best or predicted value.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Asthma is characterised by variable airflow obstruction. A single spirometry reading may be normal between attacks, so serial PEF captures the day-to-day and hour-to-hour swings in airway calibre that a one-off test misses. PEF falls when bronchial smooth muscle constricts and airways narrow, and rises after bronchodilator or during symptom-free periods.

Diagnostic support in suspected asthma when spirometry is normal or equivocal.
Home monitoring to guide a personalised self-management (action) plan.
Detecting occupational asthma via work-versus-rest patterns.
Objective severity assessment in acute attacks.
🎓 PEF is effort- and technique-dependent and reflects mainly LARGE-airway flow, so it is less sensitive to small-airway disease than FEV₁. Always interpret against the patient's own personal best, not just the population predicted value.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Correct technique is essential because a poor blow underestimates true flow:

Stand up (or sit upright); ensure the meter pointer is reset to zero.
Take a maximal deep breath in to full inflation.
Seal the lips tightly around the mouthpiece and blow out as hard and fast as possible — a short, sharp, explosive blast, not a prolonged blow.
Record the value, then repeat: take the best of 3 attempts.

For serial monitoring, the patient keeps a diary recording PEF at least twice daily (typically on waking and in the evening) for 2–4 weeks, ideally before and after bronchodilator. Each reading is the best of three blows.

3INTERPRETATION — DIURNAL VARIATION

Airways are physiologically narrowest in the early morning ("morning dipping"), so PEF is typically lowest on waking and highest in the evening. Exaggerated swings indicate variable obstruction. Diurnal variability is calculated as:

(Highest − Lowest) ÷ Highest × 100→Percentage diurnal variability over the day
Variability >20% on ≥3 days/week for 2 weeks→Supports a diagnosis of asthma (variable airflow obstruction)
Variability ≤20% / flat trace→Less supportive; does not exclude asthma — consider other tests
🌅Morning dip
Lowest reading on waking — classic asthma pattern
📈>20% swing
Threshold supporting variable obstruction
💊BD response
Rise after bronchodilator supports reversibility
🏭Work pattern
Deterioration on work days, recovery on days off

Occupational asthma: the patient keeps a diary of PEF (typically 2-hourly through waking hours) across working days and rest days/holidays. A consistent fall in PEF during work periods with recovery away from work points to a workplace sensitiser and warrants referral.

4PEF IN ACUTE ASTHMA & PITFALLS

In an acute attack, PEF is expressed as a percentage of the patient's best or predicted value and drives severity grading:

PEF ≥50–75% best/predicted→Moderate acute asthma
PEF 33–50% best/predicted→Acute SEVERE asthma (with other features e.g. can't complete sentences, RR ≥25, HR ≥110)
PEF <33% best/predicted→LIFE-THREATENING — also silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, SpO₂ <92%
A poor or sub-maximal blow underestimates PEF — check technique before acting on a low value.
Meters must be EU/EN13826-scale and readings compared on the same device.
Very sick or exhausted patients may be unable to perform PEF at all — inability to blow is itself an ominous sign.
🚩 PEF is effort-dependent, so a falsely low reading can mislead — but a genuinely low value in acute asthma is a medical emergency. PEF <50% best/predicted signals acute severe, and PEF <33% signals a LIFE-THREATENING attack requiring immediate senior help, high-flow oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and consideration of critical care.
LUNG FUNCTION__Provocation & Inflammatio:
Bronchial provocation (challenge) testing measures airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR) — the exaggerated bronchoconstrictor response that characterises asthma. It is reserved for the patient with symptoms suggestive of asthma but normal or non-diagnostic spirometry and no demonstrable bronchodilator reversibility. A controlled dose of an inhaled bronchoconstrictor (methacholine or histamine) is given and the fall in FEV₁ is tracked; a hyper-responsive airway constricts at a much lower dose than a normal one.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used chiefly to confirm or exclude asthma when the diagnosis is uncertain: typical symptoms but normal spirometry, negative reversibility, and inconclusive peak-flow variability. Methacholine is a direct challenge — it acts on muscarinic (M₃) receptors on airway smooth muscle to cause contraction, so it probes smooth-muscle responsiveness itself.

Direct agents (methacholine, histamine) act directly on smooth muscle — sensitive, high negative predictive value.
Indirect agents (mannitol, exercise, hypertonic saline) act via inflammatory mediator release — more specific for active eosinophilic asthma.
🎓 A negative methacholine challenge is most useful clinically: because of its very high negative predictive value it largely rules out current asthma in a symptomatic patient.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Withhold bronchodilators before testing (short-acting β-agonists ~8h, long-acting agents and antihistamines longer), and avoid caffeine, exercise and cold air on the day. A baseline FEV₁ is recorded; the test is only valid if baseline FEV₁ is adequate (commonly ≥60–70% predicted).

Nebulised methacholine is inhaled in doubling (serially increasing) concentrations.
FEV₁ is measured a set interval after each dose step.
The test continues until FEV₁ falls ≥20% from baseline or the maximum dose is reached.
A bronchodilator is then given to reverse the induced bronchoconstriction before discharge.
3INTERPRETATION — PC20 / PD20

The result is expressed as the PC20 (provocative concentration) or PD20 (provocative dose) of methacholine causing a 20% fall in FEV₁, interpolated from the dose–response curve. A lower PC20/PD20 means a more twitchy, hyper-responsive airway.

PC20 > 16 mg/mL→Normal — airway hyper-responsiveness effectively excluded (asthma unlikely)
PC20 4–16 mg/mL→Borderline / equivocal hyper-responsiveness
PC20 1–4 mg/mL→Mild airway hyper-responsiveness
PC20 < 1 mg/mL→Marked hyper-responsiveness — strongly supports asthma
🧪Methacholine
Direct M₃ agonist; standard UK challenge agent
💨Histamine
Alternative direct agent; more systemic side-effects (flushing, headache)
📉20% FEV₁ fall
The defining threshold for a positive response
4PITFALLS & CONTRAINDICATIONS

AHR is sensitive but not specific: a positive test also occurs in COPD, allergic rhinitis, recent viral infection, bronchiectasis and after smoking, so results must be read in clinical context. False negatives follow inadequate bronchodilator washout.

Absolute contraindications: severe airflow limitation (FEV₁ <50% predicted or <1 L), recent MI or stroke (within ~3 months), known aortic/cerebral aneurysm, uncontrolled hypertension.
Relative: moderate airflow limitation, pregnancy and breastfeeding, inability to perform reliable spirometry, current respiratory tract infection.
🚩 Bronchial provocation can precipitate severe, occasionally life-threatening bronchospasm. It must be done only where a bronchodilator, oxygen and full resuscitation facilities are immediately available, and never attempted in a patient with severe baseline airflow limitation, recent myocardial infarction/stroke, known aneurysm or during pregnancy.

Indirect bronchial provocation tests diagnose exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) and airway hyper-responsiveness by delivering a stimulus that triggers endogenous mediator release from an inflamed airway, rather than acting directly on smooth muscle. Inhaled dry-powder mannitol, standardised exercise, and eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea (EVH) all provoke airway drying/osmotic change; a defined fall in FEV₁ confirms the diagnosis and, importantly, flags the steroid-responsive inflammatory phenotype.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to confirm EIB and asthma-type airway hyper-responsiveness, especially in athletes, military recruits, and patients with exertional dyspnoea but normal resting spirometry. Direct agents (methacholine, histamine) act straight on smooth-muscle receptors and are sensitive but non-specific. Indirect stimuli work physiologically: hyperventilation of dry air, or an inhaled osmotic load, dehydrates the airway surface, raising osmolarity and triggering mast-cell and eosinophil mediator release (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes) that constricts the airway.

Indirect tests better reflect active airway inflammation.
A positive indirect test predicts a good response to inhaled corticosteroids.
More specific for asthma than methacholine; a negative test helps exclude EIB.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Withhold bronchodilators (short-acting ≥8h, long-acting ≥24-48h), caffeine, and exercise beforehand; ensure baseline FEV₁ is adequate (typically ≥70% predicted) as testing at low lung function is unsafe.

🧪Mannitol challenge
Cumulative dry-powder capsules 0→635 mg; FEV₁ measured 60s after each dose.
🏃Exercise challenge
6-8 min hard exercise to ~85% max HR breathing dry air; FEV₁ tracked to 30 min after.
💨EVH
Voluntary hyperventilation of dry gas (5% CO₂) for 6 min at high minute ventilation.

For mannitol, escalate through cumulative doses until the positive threshold is reached, a maximum dose is given, or symptoms occur. Reversibility with a bronchodilator is confirmed at the end.

3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
Exercise/EVH: ≥10% fall in FEV₁→Positive for EIB (≥15% is often used for EVH to raise specificity)
Mannitol: ≥15% fall from baseline FEV₁→Positive — airway hyper-responsiveness confirmed
Mannitol: ≥10% fall between two consecutive doses→Also counts as a positive response
PD₁₅ (dose causing 15% fall) low→Greater responsiveness = more severe/active airway inflammation
No fall at maximum dose→Negative — EIB unlikely; look for alternative cause of exertional symptoms
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Recent bronchodilator, ICS, caffeine, or a viral URTI can blunt or alter responses — false negatives.
Mannitol commonly causes cough and throat irritation; not a true bronchospastic reaction.
Exercise/EVH results depend on inspired-air dryness and achieved minute ventilation — poor effort underestimates EIB.
A negative indirect test does not exclude symptoms from other causes (e.g. inducible laryngeal obstruction, deconditioning).
🚩 Provocation testing can precipitate severe bronchospasm. Do NOT test if baseline FEV₁ is low (commonly <70% predicted) or spirometry is unstable, and never test without a bronchodilator, oxygen, and resuscitation facilities immediately available. Mannitol is contraindicated in known hypersensitivity to it or to inhaled mannitol.
🎓 High-yield: indirect challenges (mannitol, exercise, EVH) mirror airway inflammation and predict inhaled-steroid responsiveness, whereas methacholine (direct) is sensitive but non-specific. A positive mannitol test is a strong pointer that the patient will benefit from an ICS.

FeNO (fractional exhaled nitric oxide) is a quick, non-invasive breath test that measures nitric oxide in exhaled air as a surrogate marker of eosinophilic (type-2, T2-high) airway inflammation. It is used to support a diagnosis of asthma, to predict who will respond to inhaled corticosteroids, and to monitor treatment adherence — it does not measure airflow obstruction and is never used in isolation to diagnose asthma.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

In eosinophilic airway inflammation, cytokines (notably IL-13) upregulate inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS / NOS2) in bronchial epithelial cells, so more NO diffuses into the airway lumen and is exhaled. FeNO therefore rises when there is active T2-high inflammation — the type that is typically corticosteroid-responsive.

Used to support an asthma diagnosis in adults and children with suggestive symptoms.
Predicts inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) responsiveness — high FeNO favours a steroid trial.
A falling FeNO after starting ICS can confirm treatment adherence; a persistently high FeNO in a "treated" patient suggests poor adherence or technique.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The standard test is a single-breath online measurement at a constant exhalation flow of 50 mL/s, reported as FeNO₅₀ in parts per billion (ppb). The patient inhales NO-free air to total lung capacity, then exhales slowly and steadily against a fixed resistance while visual feedback keeps the flow at target; a soft-palate manoeuvre excludes nasal (high-NO) contamination.

Best done before spirometry and before bronchodilator/exercise, as forced manoeuvres can transiently lower readings.
Advise avoiding food (especially nitrate-rich), caffeine, vigorous exercise and smoking shortly before testing.
Quick, effort-dependent but achievable in most children ≥ 5 years.
3INTERPRETATION (NICE THRESHOLDS)

NICE defines a positive result at different cut-offs for adults and children. A positive FeNO adds weight to an asthma diagnosis but must be combined with symptoms and objective airflow/variability testing.

Adult FeNO ≥ 40 ppb→Positive — supports asthma diagnosis
Child (5–16 yrs) FeNO ≥ 35 ppb→Positive — supports asthma diagnosis
Value below threshold→Does NOT exclude asthma — use spirometry & other tests
High FeNO despite ICS→Consider poor adherence, poor inhaler technique or ongoing exposure
4CONFOUNDERS, PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

FeNO reflects only the eosinophilic phenotype, so it can be normal in neutrophilic or non-T2 asthma — a normal value never rules asthma out. Many factors shift the reading independently of asthma control.

⬆️Allergic rhinitis / atopy
Raises FeNO (extra eosinophilic inflammation)
🚬Smoking
Lowers FeNO (can mask true inflammation)
💊Inhaled/oral steroids
Lower FeNO (suppress iNOS)
🍗Recent food / exercise
Nitrate-rich food raises; exercise/spirometry transiently lowers
🚩 Smoking and inhaled/oral corticosteroids lower FeNO and can produce a falsely reassuring "normal" result in a patient with genuine eosinophilic inflammation. Always ask about smoking and current steroid use before interpreting the value — a low or normal FeNO never excludes asthma.
🎓 Learn the NICE cut-off: FeNO ≥ 40 ppb is positive in adults (and ≥ 35 ppb in children 5–16). A positive FeNO supports asthma and predicts inhaled-corticosteroid responsiveness, but it is one piece of the diagnostic picture — combine it with spirometry and bronchodilator reversibility or peak-flow variability.
LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Transfer & Volumes:
The transfer factor (TLCO or DLCO — the transfer/diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide) measures how efficiently gas crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane. It uses a single inhaled breath of very-low-concentration CO, which behaves like O₂ but binds haemoglobin ~250× more avidly, so its uptake is limited only by diffusion. TLCO is a whole-lung figure; KCO is TLCO corrected for the alveolar volume (VA) actually reached — the transfer factor per litre of ventilated lung — and comparing the two separates disease of the lung tissue from disease that merely restricts the lung's size.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Transfer factor assesses the integrity of the gas-exchange surface: total alveolar-capillary surface area, membrane thickness, and the volume/quality of pulmonary capillary blood. It is requested to characterise breathlessness, to distinguish emphysema (destroyed surface, low TLCO) from asthma (preserved or high TLCO) in obstruction, and to grade and monitor interstitial lung disease and pulmonary vascular disease.

CO uptake depends on diffusion across the membrane and on haemoglobin available to bind it — both are captured in a single number.
Because uptake is diffusion-limited, TLCO is exquisitely sensitive to loss of surface area or thickened membrane before spirometry changes.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The single-breath technique: the patient exhales to residual volume, then inhales a test gas (~0.3% CO plus an inert tracer such as helium or methane) rapidly to total lung capacity, holds the breath for 10 seconds, then exhales. The tracer dilution gives the alveolar volume VA; the fall in CO concentration over the breath-hold gives CO uptake, from which TLCO is derived. KCO = TLCO / VA.

Requires a cooperative patient able to achieve a full inspiration and a steady 10-second breath-hold — poor effort or air leak invalidates the result.
No smoking for ≥24 h beforehand: carboxyhaemoglobin from recent smoking occupies binding sites and falsely lowers TLCO.
A measured haemoglobin is needed to correct the result (see step 4).
3INTERPRETATION — PATTERNS

Results are expressed as % predicted; roughly 80–120% predicted is normal. The key skill is reading TLCO together with KCO and spirometry.

Low TLCO + low KCO, obstructive spirometry→Emphysema — alveolar surface destroyed
Low TLCO + low KCO, restrictive spirometry→Interstitial lung disease / pulmonary fibrosis
Low TLCO with normal spirometry & volumes→Pulmonary vascular disease (PE, pulmonary hypertension) or anaemia
Low TLCO but PRESERVED / high KCO, restrictive→Extraparenchymal restriction — chest-wall or neuromuscular (lung tissue normal, just under-inflated)
Raised TLCO (>120% predicted)→Alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, asthma, or left-to-right shunt
🫁Emphysema
Low TLCO & KCO — surface area lost
🩹Fibrosis / ILD
Low TLCO, thickened membrane
🧬PE / Pulm. vascular
Low TLCO, normal spirometry
🩸Anaemia
Falsely low unless Hb-corrected
🔴Alveolar haemorrhage
Raised TLCO — extra Hb in alveoli binds CO
💨Asthma
Normal / raised TLCO — contrast with COPD
4CORRECTING FOR Hb, PITFALLS & SAFETY

Because CO uptake depends on the amount of haemoglobin in the capillary bed, TLCO must be corrected for the patient's haemoglobin. Uncorrected, anaemia lowers and polycythaemia raises TLCO, mimicking or masking membrane disease. Modern reports use the GLI reference equations and quote Hb-corrected values.

Anaemia (low Hb)→Apparent low TLCO — correct before calling it lung disease
Polycythaemia (high Hb)→Apparent high TLCO
KCO must be interpreted with care: a small VA (incomplete inspiration, poor effort, pneumonectomy) mathematically raises KCO even when true gas exchange is impaired.
Recent smoking (raised COHb) and pregnancy also alter values.
🚩 Always Hb-correct TLCO before interpreting it — an uncorrected value in an anaemic patient can be mislabelled as fibrosis or PE. A NORMAL transfer factor does NOT exclude pulmonary embolism; TLCO is neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule out PE, so never withhold definitive imaging/anticoagulation on a normal result.
🎓 In airflow obstruction, transfer factor is the great discriminator: TLCO/KCO is reduced in emphysema (COPD) but normal or raised in asthma. Conversely, in restriction, a preserved or high KCO points to an extraparenchymal cause (chest-wall/neuromuscular) whereas a low KCO indicates intrinsic lung disease such as fibrosis.

Lung volume measurement quantifies the static volumes the lungs hold at defined points of the breathing cycle — the total gas the thorax contains and how much stays trapped after a full breath out. Simple spirometry can only measure the air a patient actively moves, so it captures VC, FEV1 and its subdivisions but never RV, FRC or TLC. Dedicated techniques — body plethysmography and gas-dilution methods (helium equilibration or nitrogen washout) — are needed to derive these absolute volumes, which then confirm true restriction (low TLC) or hyperinflation and gas trapping (raised TLC, RV and RV/TLC).

1Indication & principle: why spirometry is not enough

Spirometry measures flow at the mouth, so it can only see gas that is breathed in and out. The volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal exhalation — the residual volume (RV) — and any volume that includes it (FRC and TLC) are invisible to it. Measuring absolute volumes lets you distinguish a genuinely small lung (restriction) from a normal or large lung that empties poorly (obstruction with gas trapping).

🫁TLC
Total lung capacity — all gas after a maximal inspiration
🧪RV
Residual volume — gas left after a maximal expiration
⚖️FRC
Functional residual capacity — volume at end of quiet expiration (ERV + RV)
💨VC
Vital capacity — TLC minus RV; the only one spirometry captures
2How it is performed: plethysmography vs gas dilution

The patient sits inside a sealed, rigid body box and pants against a briefly closed shutter. As the chest compresses and expands the trapped thoracic gas, box pressure and mouth pressure change reciprocally, and Boyle's law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂) yields the thoracic gas volume at FRC. Because it senses all compressible intrathoracic gas, plethysmography includes air behind closed airways and inside bullae.

Helium dilution: the patient rebreathes a closed circuit containing a known concentration of inert helium; helium equilibrates only into communicating airspaces, and its dilution gives FRC.
Nitrogen washout: the patient breathes 100% O₂ and the exhaled nitrogen originally in the lungs is collected; the total N₂ washed out back-calculates FRC.
Derivation: both methods measure FRC first; RV = FRC − ERV, and TLC = RV + VC (slow VC measured by spirometry).
3Interpretation: restriction vs hyperinflation

TLC is the single defining number. Volumes are reported as percent predicted, and the pattern of TLC, RV and the RV/TLC ratio separates a small lung from a poorly emptying one.

TLC < 80% predicted (below lower limit of normal)→Restrictive defect (e.g. fibrosis, chest-wall or neuromuscular disease)
TLC and RV raised, RV/TLC increased→Hyperinflation with gas trapping — typical of COPD/emphysema
Low FEV₁/FVC but normal TLC→Pure obstruction without established restriction
RV/TLC ≥ ~40%→Significant air trapping
4Pitfalls & limitations

The two families of technique disagree precisely where it matters most. Gas-dilution methods only sample gas that communicates with open airways, so in severe obstruction, bullous disease or air trapping they miss the isolated pockets and underestimate RV, FRC and TLC. Plethysmography measures every compressible gas volume and reads higher — a large plethysmography-minus-dilution gap is itself a marker of trapped gas. Dilution methods also require several minutes of steady tidal breathing, which is hard for the breathless, and a mouth-seal leak invalidates the result.

🚩 In emphysema with bullae or severe gas trapping, helium dilution and nitrogen washout systematically underestimate lung volumes because they cannot access non-communicating gas — body plethysmography is the gold standard and should be used to avoid missing hyperinflation.
🎓 Learn the three patterns as one line: low TLC = restriction; normal TLC + low FEV1/FVC = obstruction; high TLC, high RV, high RV/TLC = hyperinflation with gas trapping. TLC is what turns spirometry's ratio into a diagnosis.

Airway resistance testing quantifies how hard air must be driven to flow through the conducting airways. Measured by whole-body plethysmography, it yields airway resistance (Raw) and its volume-corrected reciprocal specific airway conductance (sGaw). It objectively detects airflow obstruction — and, crucially, is effort-independent, so it remains valid when spirometry is unreliable or impossible (frail patients, poor coordination, young children).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Resistance is the driving pressure needed per unit of airflow. In obstruction (asthma, COPD, bronchiolitis) narrowed airways demand a greater pressure gradient, so Raw rises. Because resistance falls as the lungs inflate (airways are tethered open at higher volumes), Raw is meaningless without the volume at which it was measured — hence conductance (Gaw = 1/Raw) is normalised to lung volume to give sGaw = Gaw / lung volume.

Effort-independent: needs only quiet tidal panting, not a forced maximal blow.
Detects obstruction when spirometry is unreliable, poorly coordinated, or contraindicated.
Sensitive to the large/central airways and to early bronchoconstriction.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient sits inside a sealed, rigid body plethysmograph (“body box”) and breathes through a mouthpiece with a nose clip, panting gently (~1–2 breaths/second) against the flow sensor.

During panting a shutter briefly occludes the mouthpiece: mouth pressure then equals alveolar pressure.
Simultaneous box pressure changes (Boyle’s law) give the thoracic gas volume at which resistance is measured.
Raw is derived from the relationship between alveolar pressure and airflow; the same manoeuvre yields lung volume for sGaw.
3INTERPRETATION

Results are read as Raw (higher = worse) and sGaw (lower = worse), compared with predicted values.

Raw ≤ ~2.0 cmH₂O/L/s; normal sGaw→Normal airway calibre — no significant obstruction
Raw raised (> ~3 cmH₂O/L/s) with low sGaw→Airflow obstruction (asthma, COPD, bronchiolitis)
sGaw rises ≥ ~30–40% after bronchodilator→Significant reversibility — supports asthma
Raised Raw but preserved sGaw at high lung volume→Interpret with volume — hyperinflation can mask or modify the picture
🧪Raw
Airway resistance — pressure needed per unit flow; rises in obstruction
🔁Gaw
Conductance = 1/Raw; falls in obstruction
📏sGaw
Gaw normalised to lung volume; the volume-corrected index of calibre
📦Body box
Plethysmograph measuring alveolar pressure and thoracic gas volume
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Reflects mainly large/central airway resistance; small-airway disease may be underestimated.
Requires an air-tight cabin, careful calibration and a cooperative panting technique — not portable.
Air leaks, swallowing, glottic closure or an unsealed box invalidate the trace.
Always report Raw together with the lung volume; use sGaw for meaningful comparison and bronchodilator response.
🚩 Claustrophobia in the sealed box can provoke panic and hyperventilation, and inhaling a bronchial challenge agent (e.g. methacholine/histamine) to unmask obstruction risks precipitating acute bronchospasm — ensure a reversibility bronchodilator and resuscitation facilities are immediately available and avoid provocation in severe or unstable disease.
🎓 sGaw is one of the earliest and most sensitive markers of bronchoconstriction and is effort-independent — ideal for young children or anyone who cannot perform a reliable forced spirometry manoeuvre.

The Lung Clearance Index (LCI) is a measure derived from the multiple-breath washout (MBW) test. The patient breathes normally (tidal breathing) while an inert tracer gas is washed out of the lungs; the LCI quantifies how evenly gas is distributed throughout the lungs. It is a sensitive marker of ventilation inhomogeneity and small-airways disease, and detects abnormality earlier than spirometry — making it especially valuable in cystic fibrosis (CF) and early paediatric lung disease.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

LCI detects peripheral (small-airway) disease that spirometry misses. In healthy lungs an inhaled tracer distributes uniformly and clears quickly; where airways are obstructed or narrowed unevenly, some lung units empty slowly, so the tracer takes many more breaths to clear — the hallmark of ventilation inhomogeneity.

Uses an inert tracer gas: either resident nitrogen (N₂) washed out by 100% oxygen, or an exogenous gas such as sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆) washed in then out.
More sensitive and earlier than FEV₁ — abnormal LCI can be present when spirometry is still normal.
Effort-independent and performed during quiet tidal breathing, so it is feasible in young children and infants.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient sits and breathes tidally through a mouthpiece with a nose clip, connected to a gas analyser and flow meter.

Wash-in (SF₆ method): the tracer is breathed until its concentration is uniform and equilibrated across the lungs.
Washout: the patient switches to tracer-free gas (100% O₂ for the nitrogen method) and continues tidal breathing while the analyser records tracer concentration breath-by-breath.
Washout continues until the end-tidal tracer concentration falls to 1/40th (2.5%) of its starting value.
The software computes Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) from the volume of tracer eliminated, and the cumulative expired volume (CEV) needed to reach the endpoint. Several trials are averaged.
🎓 Remember the formula: LCI = CEV ÷ FRC — the number of lung-volume “turnovers” required to clear the tracer. A perfectly efficient lung needs few turnovers.
3INTERPRETATION

A higher LCI means worse ventilation distribution (more inhomogeneity). Interpret against age-appropriate reference ranges.

LCI ≤ ~7.0→Normal — even, efficient ventilation distribution
LCI > ~7.0–7.4→Abnormal — ventilation inhomogeneity / small-airways disease
Rising LCI over time→Progressive peripheral lung disease; useful for monitoring CF and treatment response
🧪FRC
Lung volume at end of tidal expiration; the denominator, derived from tracer dilution
💨CEV
Cumulative expired volume to reach 1/40th tracer; the numerator
📈LCI
Turnovers to clear tracer; rises with worsening inhomogeneity
🫁Small airways
The peripheral “silent zone” where early CF disease begins, missed by FEV₁
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Time-consuming: a single washout can take several minutes and multiple trials are needed, limiting routine clinical throughput.
Leaks and irregular breathing (mouth leak, poor nose-clip seal, coughing, swallowing) invalidate the trial and must be excluded.
Method dependence: nitrogen and SF₆ techniques give slightly different absolute values, so serial monitoring should use the same method and equipment.
Non-specific: a raised LCI signals inhomogeneity but does not identify its cause.
🚩 The nitrogen washout method delivers 100% oxygen. Prolonged high-concentration oxygen can transiently alter breathing pattern and is relevant in patients dependent on hypoxic respiratory drive; ensure appropriate monitoring and use validated protocols and reference equations.
